new_statements.quote: The domain of accent is the syllable as a whole. This means that even for long syllables (two moras of timing) the accent is born by the entire unit rather than just one or the other of the vowel segments. [...] Auye has 2 emic tones (high and low) and would probably be classified as a reduced word-tone system (contrasting on only one syllable per word) according to Donohue (1997). Besides indicating the placement of the accented syllable, the lexicon also identifies the tone assigned to the word as a whole. The assigned tone (high or low) is realized at the beginning of the word (or noun phrase) and is sustained over each succeeding syllable until the accented one is reached, after which the pitch falls gradually from high to low word-finally.
new_statements.citation: Moxness, Michael. 2011. Morphosyntactic correlates of reference in Auye: Linguistic form and narrative role in a Papuan language. SIL Electronic Working Papers 2011-003. Dallas: SIL International.

new_statements.rule_in_words: FOR AUYE (sister variety; see identity note): each word has one accented syllable whose position is lexically specified (not predictable by rule), plus a lexically assigned word tone (H or L) that spreads from the word/NP beginning up to the accented syllable, after which pitch falls to low at the word end -- i.e. a lexical accent within a reduced word-tone (pitch-accent-like) system. Certain suffixes (-taa) and the auxiliary ta/se never bear accent. No first-hand statement exists for Dao itself.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent is marked in the paper only where it distinguishes tense-aspect forms (-g IMMEDIATE vs -'g RECENT PAST 2); -taa IMPERFECTIVE and auxiliary ta/se 'do' do not take accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain of accent = syllable (long syllables carry accent as a unit); tone realized over the word or noun phrase. Statement is a brief endnote in a discourse paper, based on Moxness's unpublished 2003 Auye Grammar; it describes Auye [auu] (Siriwo river, ~500 speakers), not the Dao/Maniwo/Moi variety [daz].
new_statements.identity_note: No description of Dao [daz] itself exists (Glottolog: 0 descriptive refs; OLAC: only Glottolog/Ethnologue records). The quoted accent/tone statement is Moxness 2011 endnote 1 on AUYE [auu], glottocode auye1238, the other member of Glottolog's Auye-Dao node (auye1239). Moxness (Chan numerals page, 2008; and reportedly Auye Grammar 2003: 6-7) treats 'Maniwo' as a dialect of Auye, and Ethnologue 16 gives 75% lexical similarity Dao-Auye; Crockett (NTM, 2012) distinguishes Dao/Moi (Dao River, Napan subdistrict, 250 speakers) from 'the Maniwo dialect to the east of Auye', so even the Dao = Maniwo equation is not clean. The Auye statement should therefore be recorded under auye1238 (its./auye1238/), and applied to daoo1238 only as an inherited/inferred value, not as a first-hand Dao description.

sources.note: Endnote 1 (printed p. 42 / PDF p. 43), describing AUYE [auu], the sister variety, not Dao: accent placement is lexical ('the lexicon... indicating the placement of the accented syllable'), domain of accent is the syllable, two emic tones H/L assigned per word, 'reduced word-tone system'; pitch sustained until the accented syllable then falls to low word-finally. Also p. ~28: suffix -taa and auxiliary ta/se 'do not take accent'. Dao/Maniwo/Moi are not mentioned anywhere in the paper.
